newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak president blames government for EU failure.
newsitem.headline: Slovak president blames government for EU failure.

text.p: President Michal Kovac blamed Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's government on Thursday for Slovakia's failure to make the first round of EU enlargement and called for immediate democratic reforms.
The European Commission said on Wednesday Slovakia's record on political reforms had ruled it out of the first wave of European Union membership talks.
"The wasting of the chance Slovakia had until recently is unjustifiable," Kovac said in a broadcast.
"This has foiled the legitimate hopes and expectations for a better and more dignified future for Slovakia after decades of totalitarian past. It is an injustice committed on the future generation."

Meciar, an avowed political foe of Kovac, denied that Slovakia's absence from the list of six contenders for membership talks early next year - Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Estonia, Slovenia and Cyprus -- was a political failure.

"This is no catastrophe," Meciar said in an interview with Slovak television late on Wednesday. "This is not a final decision, only a recommendation and we still have four months in which to prepare for such a decision."
An EU summit in Luxembourg in December is to take a final decision on countries invited to EU enlargement talks.

The Commission's opinion cited government disregard for the constitution, the rights of the opposition, constant tensions between government and president and a refusal to involve the opposition in institutions including those supervising the secret service and military intelligence.
It also criticised the government for its treatment of the 500,000-strong Hungarian minority and failure to carry out a pledge made two years ago to pass a law on the use of minority languages.
Kovac called on Meciar's government to stop treating Western criticism lightly and to work immediately to introduce democratic reforms.
"If this does not happen then the government should resign and give you, the citizens of Slovakia, the chance to decide on our future in early elections," he said.

NATO last week invited just the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland to join the alliance. The government said NATO had used different crtiteria to judge Slovakia's suitabilty to those used for other aspirants.
Slovakia was seen among the frontrunners for both early EU and NATO membership when Czechoslovakia peacefully split into separate states in 1993.

But the United States and its allies have criticised Slovakia for four rocky years of opaque political infighting, problems in dealing with the Hungarian minority and major shortcomings in media and other reforms.
